clue.text: Mamet's bison

definitions.meaning: the 1975 play by David Mamet about three small-time crooks
the large shaggy wild ox of the North American plains

explanation.definitionFit: David Mamet titled his play after the North American bison, so one name covers both the play and the beast.

clue.text: Perhaps depart as one passed on

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be put in some other order, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Someone who has died is said, perhaps, to depart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' reshuffles DEPART AS; 'one' only links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means 'to the fathers', used of someone who is dead.

clue.text: Spirits did him good at Christmas

definitions.text: Spirits did him good at Christmas

parts.words: Spirits did him good at Christmas
parts.note: the ghosts of Christmas past, present and future reform Dickens's miser, not a drink doing someone good

explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' suggests drink; here they are the three ghosts of A Christmas Carol.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's miser is visited by ghosts on Christmas Eve and wakes a changed, generous man.

clue.text: Anguish was borne by her father

definitions.text: Anguish was borne by her father

parts.words: Anguish was borne by her father
parts.note: in the Tristan legend the Irish king named Anguish is this heroine's father, so 'Anguish' is a proper name, not grief

explanation.walkthrough: 'Anguish' reads as suffering; it is the name of King Anguish of Ireland in the Tristan story.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish princess loved by Tristan is the daughter of King Anguish in Malory's telling.

clue.text: Narayan described his day

parts.note: R. K. Narayan's short story 'An ... Day' describes one day of a fortune-teller

explanation.definitionFit: R. K. Narayan's best-known short story follows a street fortune-teller through a single day.

clue.text: Affectionate term of address for composer

definitions.meaning: in Wales '...' (little one) is a fond way to address someone
Johann Sebastian, the German Baroque master

explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh endearment meaning 'dear' shares its spelling with the surname of the great German Baroque musician.

clue.text: They took the blame for Scott Boswell's work

definitions.meaning: scapegoats who are made to carry the blame for others
the title of a book by the writer Scott Boswell

explanation.definitionFit: Scapegoats who carry blame are called this in American slang, which is also the title of Boswell's book.

clue.text: Positive Sheridan character arranges any as buttonhole

indicators.note: arranges says the letters of the following words are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A dandy character in a Sheridan comedy fixes a flower in his lapel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Positive' points at the surname: absolute means positive, certain. The irascible father in Sheridan's The Rivals.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Anthony is the choleric father in Sheridan's The Rivals, his surname a synonym of 'certain'.

clue.text: Iroquois language for a single Gilbertian princess

parts.note: a single thing is one
Princess Ida is the heroine of the Gilbert and Sullivan opera of that name

explanation.surface: A linguist hunts for a word in an Iroquois tongue fit for one of Gilbert's princesses.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oneida are one of the Six Nations of the Iroquois, and their tongue bears the people's name.

clue.text: Before very old saint started for and against

parts.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before

explanation.surface: A very old saint once launched a debate, arguing both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: the Abbé Prévost founded the periodical Le Pour et Contre, 'for and against'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French novelist of Manon Lescaut founded a journal titled 'Le Pour et Contre'.

clue.text: Allow in French side to meet novelist

indicators.note: in puts the word for allow inside the French word for side

parts.note: côté is French for side
to let is to allow

explanation.surface: A French team is permitted to meet a writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Sidonie-Gabrielle, author of Gigi and the Claudine books, was a French writer of fiction.

clue.text: Prince Myshkin

parts.note: the gentle, epileptic hero of Dostoevsky's novel, who gives the book its title

explanation.definitionFit: Dostoevsky named his novel after its innocent hero, Prince Myshkin, whom society thinks a simpleton.

clue.text: Like Amy Clampitt's figure?

parts.note: Amy Clampitt's collection 'Archaic Figure' calls its figure archaic, i.e. ancient

explanation.definitionFit: Clampitt's book is titled Archaic Figure, and archaic means very ancient, of long standing.

clue.text: Bond creation who knew his station in life

definitions.text: Bond creation who knew his station in life

parts.words: Bond creation who knew his station in life
parts.note: Michael Bond's bear is named after the London railway station where he was found

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' suggests 007; it is Michael Bond, and 'station' is a literal railway terminus in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Michael Bond's bear from Peru was found at a London railway terminus and named after it.

clue.text: Audibly positive votes for seers?

indicators.note: audibly means the word for the votes is taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: the ayes are those voting yes

explanation.surface: Votes in favour are cast out loud for prophets.
explanation.definitionFit: Organs of sight are things that see, so in a playful sense they are seers.

clue.text: Borrow sequel, with interest, for travelling gentleman

definitions.meaning: Romani for a gentleman who keeps company with gypsies

explanation.definitionFit: George Borrow's follow-up to Lavengro takes its title from the Romani phrase for a gypsy gentleman.

clue.text: French shepherd with current television series set offshore

parts.note: berger is French for shepherd
AC is alternating current

explanation.surface: A French herdsman and an electrical current feature in a TV drama filmed on an island.
explanation.walkthrough: BERGERAC was a BBC detective drama set on Jersey, a Channel Island off the coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The BBC detective drama about Jim Bergerac was set on Jersey in the Channel Islands.

clue.text: Latest information at high point in novel language

parts.note: news is the latest information
a peak is a high point

explanation.surface: Fresh tidings arrive at the summit in a strange tongue.
explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four invents the party's pared-down tongue; 'novel' means from a book.

clue.text: Calling for

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Calling for' is cut short (likely a cross-reference to 9 across, Prévost): nothing in it defines or builds the answer.

clue.text: "I hear the — Curfeu sound, Over some wide-water'd shore" (Milton, Il Penseroso)

definitions.text: "I hear the — Curfeu sound, Over some wide-water'd shore" (Milton, Il Penseroso)

parts.words: "I hear the — Curfeu sound, Over some wide-water'd shore" (Milton, Il Penseroso)
parts.note: the missing word in Milton's line describes the distant curfew bell heard across the water

explanation.definitionFit: Milton's speaker hears the curfew bell from a great distance, across a wide shore.

clue.text: Go to doctor in charge to find Pulitzer nominated work

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Seeing the doctor in charge to find a prize-shortlisted book.
explanation.definitionFit: Frederick Buechner's novel about a medieval hermit-saint was a finalist for the 1981 Pulitzer Prize.

clue.text: Gold costume a suitable disguise for charioteer

parts.note: AU is the chemical symbol for gold
a rig is an outfit or costume

explanation.surface: A gold outfit makes a fitting disguise for a chariot driver.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the northern constellation whose name is Latin for 'the charioteer'.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern constellation is pictured as a chariot driver, and its Latin name means exactly that.

clue.text: Fair-handed Spring every grace " (James Thomson)

parts.note: the gap in Thomson's line from The Seasons is the verb for Spring revealing and pouring out its graces

explanation.definitionFit: Thomson's Spring opens her heart and reveals her graces, as one confides by baring the breast.

clue.text: Twenty choirs we hear, found in English literature, amply portrayed

definitions.note: twenty quires of paper, and 'quires' is said like 'choirs'

indicators.note: found in says the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Twenty choral groups are depicted at length in English writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' marks the run 'literatuRE AMply'; 'we hear' turns 'choirs' into quires, sheets of paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Paper is counted in quires of 24 or 25 sheets, and twenty of those make one bundle of about 500.

clue.text: Joyce's father (a Dubliner)

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held 'Joyce's father (a Dubliner)' does not lead to O'ROURKE: no source ties Joyce's father to the name, so the clue seems garbled or cut short.

clue.text: Instrument of sadism, among the misfortunes of virtue

definitions.text: Instrument of sadism, among the misfortunes of virtue

parts.words: Instrument of sadism, among the misfortunes of virtue
parts.note: de Sade's Justine, or the Misfortunes of Virtue, puts its heroine through cruelty of every kind

explanation.walkthrough: 'sadism' is a nod to the Marquis de Sade, whose novel's subtitle is 'the Misfortunes of Virtue'.
explanation.definitionFit: Infliction of severe pain is the sadist's tool, and Justine suffers it repeatedly in de Sade's novel.

clue.text: Lady Browning's take on Cornish waterway?

definitions.text: Lady Browning's take on Cornish waterway?

parts.words: Lady Browning's take on Cornish waterway?
parts.note: Daphne du Maurier was Lady Browning by marriage; her 1941 novel is named after a Helford river inlet

explanation.walkthrough: Lady Browning is Daphne du Maurier, wife of General Sir Frederick Browning; the novel is named for an inlet in Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: Du Maurier's romance of a Breton pirate takes its title from a real tidal inlet off the Helford River.
